extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Francis Bacon, early‑modern intellectual history, and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Close textual and historical interpretation of Francis Bacon's religious opinions, including comparison of his writings across time, clarification of key terms (e.g., 'form'), and assessment of his theological attitudes (toleration, indifference, separation of science and religion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare primary texts and dated references
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare passages across Bacon's works (Novum Organum, De Augmentis, Essays, Confession of Faith, etc.) to form an independent opinion on his religious stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asks the reader to 'carefully compare the following references' (Nov. Org. i.65, 89; De Augmentis lib. i, iii.2, iii.4, ix.; Essays; Bacon's Confession of Faith). Pay attention to publication and manuscript dates (e.g., the Confession first appeared in Remains 1648 but was written before summer 1603) since dating affects interpretation and may show earlier vs later positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess sincerity and conformity to contemporary doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether Bacon's religious statements express his sincere convictions and whether he materially dissented from the fundamental doctrines of Christianity current in his day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text concludes that 'the religious side of these Aphorisms expresses Bacon's sincere convictions' and that he 'did not materially dissent from the religious teaching...on the fundamental doctrines.' Use internal textual evidence and comparison with contemporary doctrine to judge sincerity and conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect changes via omissions and variations between editions
rubrics_metrics.description: Note omissions or alterations between earlier and later works as possible evidence of changing views or reluctance to enter into doctrinal detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a passage on the nature and attributes of God in the Advancement of Learning is omitted in the De Augmentis published 18 years later. Such omissions may indicate later reticence or a shift in emphasis and should be weighed alongside other evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate degree and limits of toleration
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine Bacon's stance on religious toleration, including what extremes he rejected and what limits he likely would have set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use essays such as 'Of Unity in Religion' to show Bacon's avoidance of both zealot absolutism and lukewarm accommodation. The author suggests Bacon favored wide toleration but might have set limits (e.g., excluding 'Papists' and 'Atheists' as Locke later did). Examine passages about means of procuring unity and cautions against forceful propagation of religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish intellectual indifference from heartfelt indifference
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between an author's skepticism of theological disputation as an intellectual judgement and a deeper 'indifference of the heart' or lack of religious enthusiasm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues Bacon's indifference 'was not simply an indifference of the head; it was an indifference of the heart' — he respected religion but prioritized science. Look for statements about his priorities (advance of science, seeking God in nature) and for tone indicating lack of enthusiasm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess preference for atheism over superstition and political consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze Bacon's preference for the dangers of atheism versus the greater dangers of superstition, and the political/social implications he draws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bacon writes 'It were better to have no opinion of God at all, than such an opinion as is unworthy of him.' The guidance discusses how superstition 'hath been the confusion of many states' and that recoil from Roman superstition shaped seventeenth‑century views. Use this to evaluate Bacon's political reasoning about religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the declared separation of the spheres of science and theology
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine Bacon's argument that Reason and Faith belong to distinct spheres (give to reason the things of reason, to faith the things of faith) and assess its implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key passages: Novum Organum and De Augmentis where Bacon recommends putting science and theology asunder so that 'the one would declare the Will of God, and the other His Power.' Consider how this 'truce' affects the use of Scripture and reason, and trace its influence on successors (Hobbes, Pascal, Locke, Hume).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify technical vocabulary through comprehensive textual collection ('form')
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect and carefully analyze all important passages where Bacon defines or uses the term 'form' to determine its shades of meaning and underlying conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §8 emphasizes the difficulty of defining 'Form' in Novum Organum and De Augmentis. The method is to 'collect the more important passages' and compare usages (e.g., form as 'differentia vera', 'definitio vera', law of acts, or 'ipsissima res'). Also consult Aristotelian Four Causes as background. Note distinctions between simple and compound forms and the program of discovering 'simplex rerum formae' (few in number, combinable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical context and history of opinion to interpret statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Place Bacon's statements within the intellectual and political context of his age (religious disputes, Synod of Dort, recoil from Roman superstition) to understand motives and likely interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author repeatedly appeals to the 'history of opinion' and to events and tendencies of the seventeenth century to explain why Bacon wrote as he did. Factor in contemporary controversies, popular attitudes, and subsequent historical developments when interpreting passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate verbal quibbles from substantive doctrinal differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize meaning over fixed terms: identify when disagreements are largely terminological rather than substantive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted maxim: 'Men create oppositions which are not; and put them into new terms so fixed, as whereas the meaning ought to govern the term, the term in effect governeth the meaning.' When assessing disputes, determine whether disputants mean the same thing despite different language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace influence on later thinkers and weigh intellectual consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess how Bacon's positions (e.g., separation of faith and reason, tolerance) influenced later philosophers and the development of science and theology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text links Bacon's teachings to Hobbes (religion to magistrate), Pascal (divorce between faith and reason), Locke (toleration boundaries), and others. Use comparative analysis to map tendencies and unintended consequences of Bacon's views.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about imposing anachronistic questions (e.g., authority of Scripture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and respect the intellectual assumptions of Bacon's era (for instance, acceptance of Scripture's authority) and avoid expecting Bacon to have raised questions that were not customary then.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes 'that it did not occur to Bacon to ask what grounds the authority of Scripture itself reposed' and that men of that age 'were not in the habit of putting' such questions. Interpret Bacon within his epistemic frame rather than by later standards.
